title: Proposal Storyboard Structure That Holds Through Red Team
summary: October 2026 guide to building proposal storyboards that keep win themes and proof points intact at Red Team.
body_markdown:
A proposal storyboard that holds through Red Team isn't built from a good outline. It's built from a row-by-row argument, where every section traces to a Section M criterion, every win theme has a proof point attached, and capture intelligence actually made it from the black hat session into the draft. Here's what that structure looks like before anyone writes a word.


**TLDR:**


- A proposal storyboard maps each section to its Section L instruction, Section M criterion, win theme, and named proof point before any prose gets written.
- Storyboards fail Red Team when win themes stay in BD notes and never get translated into section-level arguments with attached proof points.
- Every storyboard row must answer three questions before drafting: what Section L requires, what Section M scores, and what proof point closes the gap.
- Ghost strategy columns should never sit blank where competitive intelligence exists; black hat findings belong in specific rows, not slide decks.
- GovEagle parses Section L and Section M requirements from the RFP and generates a pre-mapped a compliance matrix in Excel and an annotated outline in Word.


## What a Proposal Storyboard Actually Is in GovCon


A proposal storyboard is a section-by-section blueprint built before any prose gets written. Each row maps a proposal section to its governing[Section L instruction](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/section-l-instructions-conditions-and-notices-to-bidders) , its corresponding Section M evaluation criterion, the win theme it carries, the discriminators that separate your firm from competitors, and the proof points that substantiate the claim. Nothing in the storyboard is narrative yet. It is structured argument in column form.


That distinction matters. A generic outline tells writers what sections to write. A storyboard tells them what each section must prove, to whom, and with what evidence. Without that scaffolding, writers make judgment calls about emphasis that may not survive a Red Team review where evaluators score against[Section M evaluation factors](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/section-m-evaluation-factors-for-award) , not intuition.


Consider the difference in practice. An outline row might read: *3.2 Program Management Approach.* A storyboard row for the same section reads: Section L requires a description of management structure and reporting lines; Section M scores it under “proven program management experience” as the most important technical subfactor; the response approach is to show how a dedicated PM with embedded oversight reduced schedule risk on a comparable DHS task order; the proof point is Contract No. HSHQDC-22-F-0041, delivered on time across all milestones. The outline tells a writer what to title the section. The storyboard tells them what argument wins it.


The storyboard also connects capture strategy to proposal execution. Win themes gathered during capture, competitive intelligence from black hat analysis, and pricing assumptions from price-to-win work all belong in the storyboard before the annotated outline is built. When that handoff is skipped, the proposal reflects the writer's understanding of the opportunity, not the capture team's.


## Why Storyboards Fail the Red Team


Red Team should score the draft the way evaluators will, not rebuild the strategy behind it. When reviewers spend the session rewriting strategy, debating win themes, or questioning whether a section responds to the evaluation criterion, the storyboard failed before a single word was drafted.


The most common cause:[win themes](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/win-themes) that exist in BD notes but never got translated into section-level assignments. Each storyboard section needs its own argument, not a restatement of the firm-wide win theme. "We have deep agency relationships" is a BD talking point. "Our three prior DHS task orders of comparable scope confirm on-time delivery at scale" is a section-level story with a proof point attached.


Missing Section M traceability is the other consistent failure mode. Storyboard rows that reference Section L instructions but ignore how evaluators will score the response leave writers guessing at emphasis. Red Team reviewers then flag sections as "not compelling" when the real problem is structural: the section was never mapped to the criterion it needed to satisfy.


Other patterns that regularly surface at Red Team:


- Capture intelligence that stayed in the CRM and never reached the storyboard
- Discriminators listed without a ghost strategy connecting them to a specific competitor weakness
- Proof points referenced by project name but not matched to the relevant evaluation factor
- Price-to-win assumptions that influenced the technical approach but aren't visible in the storyboard row


If reviewers are making strategy calls at Red Team, that work was due three weeks earlier.


## Anchoring the Storyboard to Section L and Section M


Section L defines the container. Section M defines what has to live inside it. A storyboard that conflates the two produces sections that are compliant in structure but weak on[evaluation merit](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-48/chapter-1/subchapter-C/part-15/subpart-15.3/section-15.304) , and Red Team will catch the difference. Task orders and GSA buys often skip the uniform contract format, but the same logic applies: map the instructions to whatever the solicitation says it will evaluate.


Map each Section L instruction to a storyboard row first. That step is mechanical. Where teams lose ground is failing to pull the corresponding Section M criterion into the same row. If Section M lists "proven program management experience" as the most important technical subfactor, every storyboard row touching management approach needs to be built backward from that criterion, not forward from the instruction.


Every storyboard row should answer three questions before a writer touches it: what Section L requires the section to include, what Section M says evaluators will score, and what proof point closes the gap between the two.


If a row cannot answer all three, it is not ready for drafting. Traceability to a specific evaluation factor belongs in the storyboard. Treating Section M as a checklist to revisit at Gold Team means rebuilding sections around evaluation criteria at the point where rewriting the argument is the only option, not editing prose.


## Translating Capture Intelligence into Section-Level Stories


Capture teams build relationship maps, run black hat sessions, develop price-to-win positions, and document customer hot buttons. Then an RFP drops and most of that intelligence gets summarized onto a win theme slide that sits in the kickoff deck and never appears again.


A win theme without a section assignment is a slogan. "Best value at lowest risk" posted on a kickoff slide does not help a writer staring at the past performance volume. The storyboard is where that theme becomes actionable: which section carries it, which Section M criterion it maps to, and which contract award proves it.


The translation work is column-by-column:


- Win themes move from the capture deck into specific storyboard rows, tied to the Section L instruction they satisfy.
- Black hat findings get converted into ghost strategies assigned to the sections where a competitor's weakness is most exploitable.
- Customer hot buttons and agency priorities become[discriminators](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/discriminators) with named proof points, not adjectives.


Price-to-win assumptions need the same treatment. If PTW analysis shifted your technical approach toward a leaner staffing model, that assumption belongs in the management approach row. Otherwise Red Team reviewers will question the staffing rationale without knowing it was an intentional competitive decision.


The test: can a writer who was not in the capture phase read a single row and understand what the section must argue, why it matters to this evaluator, and what proof closes the case? If not, the intelligence is still trapped in capture.


## The Anatomy of a Strong Storyboard Row


Every storyboard row is a compressed proposal argument. If any field is blank, the section is not ready to draft.


Field What Goes Here


Section L Instruction The instruction governing what this section must contain


Section M Criterion The evaluation factor or subfactor this section will be scored against


Response Approach The argument the section will make, in one or two sentences


Win Theme / Discriminator The specific differentiator this section carries, not the firm-wide theme


Proof Point Named contract, metric, or past performance reference tied to the evaluation factor


Ghost Strategy Competitor weakness this section exploits, or 'none identified'


Author The SME or writer responsible for the first draft


A row that fills every column is draftable; Ghost Strategy can read "none identified" only when black hat analysis found nothing relevant to this section. A row with a blank proof point or a ghost strategy listed as "TBD" is a Red Team problem waiting to happen. The response approach column is where most storyboards go thin: "describe our PM approach" is not an argument. "Show how our dedicated PM structure reduced schedule risk on a comparable DHS task order" is.


## Ghosting the Competition Inside the Storyboard


Ghosting works when the evaluator scores your section higher without knowing why the comparison occurred to them. The storyboard is where that effect gets designed, not improvised during drafting.


The technique is straightforward in theory: identify a competitor's weakness, then structure your section's argument so that satisfying the evaluation criterion also implicitly surfaces that weakness as a risk. If a competitor runs lean on senior labor during the first 90 days, your management approach row includes proof of your transition-phase staffing ratios. You never name the competitor. The evaluator scores the section and carries the contrast forward.


At the storyboard level, the Ghost Strategy column should never be left blank on sections where competitive intelligence exists. Black hat findings from capture should map directly to specific rows, not sit in a slide deck. For each identified competitor weakness, the storyboard should answer two questions: which section is the right vehicle, and what proof point makes the contrast land without stating it?


A few patterns worth building into the storyboard review:


- If a competitor's past performance shows schedule overruns on similar work, your ghost goes in the past performance row, anchored to on-time delivery metrics from contracts with comparable scope.
- If a competitor typically proposes a centralized management structure for distributed task work, your ghost goes in the management approach row, with a staffing chart showing embedded oversight at the task level.
- If their price position is known to run high, your PTW assumptions inform the cost volume row's framing around value delivery, not cost reduction.


A writer who sees a populated Ghost Strategy column knows the section has to do two things: satisfy Section M and leave the evaluator with an unanswered question about any alternative approach that doesn't match yours.

## Running a Storyboard Review Before Red Team


Whether your shop calls it a storyboard review or folds it into an early[Pink Team](https://www.goveagle.com/blog/pink-red-gold-team-reviews-playbook) , it happens before prose exists, so reviewers are checking whether every row is ready to produce draftable direction, not editing writing.


Keep attendance narrow: the capture lead, proposal manager, and one subject matter expert who can validate proof points. A room full of stakeholders produces wordsmithing on a document that doesn't exist yet.


The review runs four questions, row by row:


- Does this row trace to a specific Section M evaluation factor, or only a Section L instruction?
- Is the win theme or discriminator distinct from the firm-wide theme, or a restatement of it?
- Is the proof point named and matched to the right evaluation factor, or listed as "past performance TBD"?
- Does the ghost strategy reference a specific finding from black hat analysis, or is it generic?


Any row that fails one of those checks gets flagged before the annotated outline is built. Closing gaps at this stage takes minutes, especially when teams follow a structured[compliance matrix guide](https://www.goveagle.com/blog/compliance-matrix-guide-how-to-build) ; closing them after a writer has drafted the section takes a full Red Team cycle. Red Team should never be the first time someone asks whether a section's argument ties to how evaluators will score it.


## Connecting the Storyboard to the Annotated Outline


The storyboard is a planning document. The[annotated outline](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/annotated-outline) is where writers actually work. The handoff between them is where requirement traceability either survives or gets quietly abandoned.


When a finalized storyboard row moves into the annotated outline in Word, it should carry its full argument with it: the Section L instruction, the Section M criterion, the response approach, the win theme, the proof point, the ghost strategy, and the author assignment.


A section header with nothing beneath it except "write about our PM experience" loses everything the storyboard built, and the writer starts from scratch instead of from a structured argument.


Each annotated section should enter drafting pre-loaded with the row's core direction: what the section must prove, which evaluation factor it maps to, and what named proof point closes the argument. Author assignments move with it, so there is no ambiguity about who owns the draft or what position they are defending.


If a reviewer cannot open the annotated outline and trace a section's pre-draft instructions back to a specific Section L instruction and Section M criterion without returning to the storyboard, the handoff was incomplete and the compliance thread is broken before drafting begins.


## How AI Tools Change the Storyboard Workflow


AI tools change where time goes in storyboard development, not whether the work gets done.


The mechanical parts of storyboard setup accelerate meaningfully. RFP parsing tools can extract Section L instructions and Section M evaluation factors in minutes, pre-populating the storyboard's requirement and evaluation columns before anyone has read the full solicitation. Semantic search against past proposal libraries can surface relevant proof points, matching contract history to specific task areas instead of relying on a writer to remember the right project. AI can also suggest candidate[win themes](https://www.goveagle.com/blog/capture-win-themes-proposal-volumes) drawn from the RFP's stated agency priorities, giving the capture lead a starting point instead of a blank row.


Where AI stops is exactly where the storyboard's value is highest. Ghost strategy requires competitive intelligence from[black hat analysis](https://www.goveagle.com/blog/black-hat-federal-proposal-strategy) and human judgment about which section is the right vehicle. Customer relationship framing depends on context that lives in the capture lead's head, not a document library. Pricing-aligned narrative, where price-to-win assumptions have shaped the technical approach, requires someone who was in the room when those tradeoffs were made. No amount of requirement extraction produces that.


The practical result: AI-assisted storyboard workflows tend to close the gap on structural setup while capture and proposal teams focus on argument quality. The rows arrive pre-loaded with references; the judgment about what each row must prove stays a human decision.


## Common Storyboard Mistakes That Surface at Red Team


These patterns appear at Red Team often enough to treat as a standing checklist.


- Win themes that describe assumed capabilities: "experienced team," "proven methodology," or "commitment to quality" tell an evaluator nothing a competitor couldn't also claim. A discriminator must be specific to your firm and verifiable against Section M criteria.
- Proof points listed by project name without connecting the contract's scope, scale, or outcome to the evaluation factor being scored.
- Section M gaps where a row maps to a Section L instruction but carries no corresponding evaluation criterion, so the section gets written but does not score well.
- Ghost strategies marked as "TBD" or left blank because black hat findings never reached the storyboard before writing began.
- Author assignments made without briefing the writer on the win theme logic or ghost strategy, producing technically accurate prose that argues the wrong thing.


Each of these is a storyboard gap, not a writing failure. When Red Team reviewers flag a section as "not compelling," they are typically identifying a row that was never finished.

## Final Thoughts on Turning Proposal Storyboards Into a Competitive Advantage


Your storyboard is the one place where capture intelligence, Section M criteria, and ghost strategies either come together or stay siloed. When a row cannot answer what the section must prove, which evaluation factor it maps to, and what named proof point closes the argument, your Red Team will answer those questions for you, at the point where rewriting is the only option left. Treating the storyboard as a compressed proposal argument, not an outline, is what separates proposals that score well from ones that read well but miss the mark, and that holds regardless of the tools in use.


## FAQ


### What should a proposal storyboard row include before a writer is allowed to start drafting?


Every storyboard row needs seven fields before it is draftable, in this order: (1) the Section L instruction governing the section, (2) the corresponding Section M evaluation criterion, (3) the response approach the section will argue, (4) the win theme or discriminator specific to that section (not the firm-wide theme), (5) a named proof point tied to the evaluation factor, (6) a ghost strategy drawn from black hat findings, and (7) an author assignment. Ghost Strategy may read "none identified" only when black hat analysis found nothing relevant to that section; "TBD" or a blank field is not acceptable. A row with any blank or vague field, especially a vague proof point or an unsupported ghost strategy entry, will surface as a Red Team problem, not a writing problem.


### How do I translate capture intelligence from a CRM or kickoff deck into a proposal storyboard?


Move each capture artifact into a specific storyboard column before the annotated outline is built: win themes from the capture deck go into individual rows tied to the Section L instruction they satisfy, black hat findings become ghost strategies assigned to the sections where a competitor's weakness is most exploitable, and price-to-win assumptions that shaped the technical approach belong in the management approach row so Red Team reviewers understand they were intentional competitive decisions, not drafting gaps. If a writer who was not in the capture phase cannot read a single row and understand what the section must argue, why it matters to this evaluator, and what proof closes the case, the intelligence is still trapped in capture.


### What is the difference between a Section L instruction and a Section M evaluation criterion in a proposal storyboard?


Section L defines what the proposal must contain; Section M defines how evaluators will score what it contains. A storyboard row that maps only to Section L produces a section that is structurally compliant but may score poorly because it was never built backward from the evaluation factor. Every row should answer both: what does Section L require this section to include, and what does Section M say evaluators will score against it.


### How does GovEagle change storyboard setup compared to building it manually in Word?


The structural work stays the same; where time goes changes. GovEagle parses Section L and Section M requirements directly from the RFP, generating a compliance matrix in Excel and an annotated outline in Word with sections pre-mapped to governing instructions and evaluation criteria before drafting begins. Win themes, ghost strategies, and proof point selection remain the capture and proposal team's call; GovEagle handles the structural setup so that work starts sooner. Manual builds require teams to shred the RFP by hand and redo that work when amendments arrive. In GovEagle, amendments are uploaded to the solicitation package so requirement extraction reflects the current solicitation.


### What causes a proposal storyboard to fail a Red Team review before any prose is written?


The most consistent failure modes are win themes that were never assigned to specific sections, Section M evaluation criteria missing from storyboard rows that only reference Section L instructions, proof points listed by project name without connecting scope or outcomes to the relevant evaluation factor, and ghost strategies left blank because black hat findings stayed in a slide deck instead of reaching the storyboard. When Red Team reviewers flag a section as "not compelling," they are typically identifying a row that was never finished: the writing problem is actually a a planning gap that was caught too late to fix without a full review cycle.
